persons.note: A CONTEMPORARY CHICAGO PAPER OF 1833-1835 PRINTS THIS PERSON BY NAME IN THE TOWN. Read from directory_1844, newspaper_1833_1835. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G1b), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. newspaper_1833_1835 names this person at Chicago by 29 October 1834 and nothing says when they came. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the person was at Chicago by 1 July 1835 on this record's own evidence. No figure is drawn (L1). THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 2 times, as “LLOYD ALEXANDER”, 1833-10-22 to 1833-10-25: 2 parcels of the school section — lot 1 of block 25 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 3 of block 118 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 0.00 acres stated in all, for $231.00 (ls0279, ls0280). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: LLOYD ALEXANDER matches Alexander Lloyd: the forename names Alexander Lloyd of the 1 person of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

book_evidence.locator: res Wells b Lake and Randolph sts

roles.note: A TRADE PRINTED AGAINST THIS NAME IN A LATER VOLUME, and this row says which year rather than leaving it to a pointer (T-0693, carried here by tools/derive_resident_roles.py). `role` is null because the directory's wording has not been adjudicated into the closed vocabulary — the printing is what the source gives and the printing is what is kept. T-1254 is where the controlled term is ruled on. It is not a claim about 1835-07-01 and never becomes one: the year is 1844. SYNONYM-FOLDED (T-1254): the same source prints this role as builder, of L. Blakesly & Co as well, and one source asserting one role over one bound is one row.

merge_ruling.for_merge: THIS IS THE STRONGEST MERGE ARGUMENT IN THE FORTY-THREE AND IT IS RECORDED IN FULL. Two consecutive directories print the same man's trade, firm and street under the two spellings: Fergus 1843 has 'Loyd, Alexander, carpenter and builder, (L., Blakesley & Co.), res 52 Wells [4th mayor…]' and Norris 1844 has 'Lloyd, Alexander, builder, of L. Blakesly & Co. res Wells b Lake and Randolph sts'. Same given name, same trade, same firm, same street. Moses & Kirkland's History sets both spellings inside one work and for one man — v1 indexes 'Loyd, Alexander, 102' and prints 'Alexander Lloyd' at four places, v2 prints 'Alexander Loyd, Mayor of the city' and 'with Alexander Lloyd for the building of…' — and the Democrat prints 'A. Lloyd' on 29 October 1834 and 'A. Loyd' on 19 November 1834, three weeks apart. The firm and the address are NON-NAME discriminators and they agree; the town is carrying its own fourth mayor as two residents.
merge_ruling.against_merge: AND IT IS STILL REFUSED HERE, BECAUSE NO LANDED RULE REACHES IT AND THIS PASS MAY NOT WRITE ONE. C9 wants one publication caught setting both spellings for one man INSIDE THE WINDOW: the Democrat's two settings are two different issues, and Moses & Kirkland is an 1895 history describing 1840, so the catch is outside the window and its v2 index besides carries a 'Lloyd, Alexander C., 384' whose middle initial neither card has. C11 is the rule this evidence actually fits — two spellings discharging one documented office, tied by a non-name discriminator — but C11 as drafted requires THE SURNAME TO AGREE LETTER FOR LETTER and varies the forename, and it is the surname that varies here. That asymmetry is the same one C14 was written to fix for C12, and fixing it for C11 is a new MERGE rule. T-1027 is explicit that the one-letter pool may not be closed by widening the join, and a merge is a card DELETION that moves the town's count; drawing a rule to make one is the owner's call and not this pass's. So the argument is kept verbatim, as D7 requires, and the cards stay two.

associated_with.note: GROUND HE BOUGHT, WHICH IS NOT GROUND HE STOOD ON — the rung is `tract` for that reason, and `land_purchased` is in neither the home kinds nor the work kinds because a holding is not a place a man was. The federal tract-sale register carries 2 row(s) — ls0279, ls0280 — to this purchaser, read as 'LLOYD ALEXANDER', sorted onto school_section by tools/sort_land_sales_onto_tracts.py and covering about 5.68 acre(s) of it. THE TIER IS INFERRED AND THE TWO HALVES DIFFER: the purchase is documented — the register is a public record and states it — while the tie between that purchaser and THIS card is an identity ruling, upheld under T-0850 on 2026-09-10 by the rule 'LLOYD ALEXANDER matches Alexander Lloyd: the forename names Alexander Lloyd of the 1 person of this surname, and the forename agrees in full.'. The weaker half sets the tier. `to` is null because the register records a sale and not a tenure.

research_note: MINTED FROM THE CONSOLIDATED CIVIC, CHURCH, PRESS, BOOK AND CENSUS EVIDENCE (T-0513, T-0514). THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER, NOT AN ARGUMENT: every other record here is written unattested in its own block, because the lists that name this person name a person and not a family. What is claimed is that the sources cited on the member below name them at Chicago, and the grade is the owner's ratified ladder applied by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py --build and spent by tools/mint_civic_residents.py, which prints every refusal. docs/LIBERTIES.md L215 carries the liberty and the tension with L213.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. residence_back_projection.note: A LATER HOME ADDRESS, READ BACKWARDS 9 YEARS. The street is not an 1835 reading: Norris's Chicago directory of 1844 printed where this person lived in 1844, and this pass carries it back to the scene date because nothing in the 1835 corpus says where the house stood. What is claimed is the street FACE and nothing narrower — no lot, no roof, no door count, and no corner even where the volume prints one — and the grade is `reconstructed`, this dataset's word for a figure the reconstruction supplies rather than a source. Wells Street stands in 1835 under that name and in that place, and the entry prints it as this person's home. The volume narrows it further — it names Lake Street and Randolph Street — and clause R5 declines to take the point: a corner or a run between two crossings is a fact about the numbered grid of the 1840s, and a house moves more than a shopfront does. So the placement is the FACE and nothing narrower, and no roof is dealt. A home is carried back on a weaker argument than a shop is: a shopfront is capital sunk into one street's trade and a lodging is a month's rent, which is why this policy claims less than docs/ADDRESS-BACK-PROJECTION.md does from the same volume. The rule is docs/RESIDENCE-BACK-PROJECTION.md and the liberty is L223; a reader who thinks 9 years is too far to carry a house should read the grade as the disagreement being invited.
